auditMetadata.scope: All backend services under backend/services/ + backend/src/ shared routes + backend/services/api-gateway/
auditMetadata.existingDedupeTicketsChecked: 300+ tickets in dedupe_index.json (R5.BE.001-025, LIVE.BE.*, LIVE.GW.*, LIVE.DB.*, LIVE.AUTH.*, LIVE.R4.*, LIVE.BIZ.*, LIVE.CONFIG.*)
auditMetadata.dedupeMethod: Grep pattern matching against dedupe_index.json for each finding, cross-referencing R5.BE.001-025 (all status=done)

findings.title: auth-service internal routes have NO authentication middleware allowing any network-adjacent caller to create/delete users and assign roles
findings.dedupeCheck: Searched 'internal.*no.*auth', 'auth.*internal.*no.*guard', 'service.*to.*service.*no.*auth' — no matches in dedupe_index.json. R5.BE.001 covers inventory transactions, R5.BE.002 covers GRN receive, R5.BE.003 covers platform stores — none cover auth-service internal routes.
findings.description: The auth-service internal.ts router (line 30) has NO authentication middleware whatsoever. All 15+ endpoints (POST /users, DELETE /users/:id, POST /users/:id/roles, DELETE /users/:id/roles/:roleName, POST /roles, PATCH /roles/:id, DELETE /roles/:id, POST /users/verify) are fully open. While the intent is 'service-to-service only', there is no service token validation, no API key check, no IP allowlist — any caller that can reach the auth-service network port can create admin users, assign arbitrary roles, delete users, and verify credentials. In a Cloud Run deployment where services share the same VPC, any compromised service or misconfigured ingress exposes the entire user/role system.
findings.evidence: Line 30: `const router: Router = Router();` — no middleware applied. Line 70-77: `router.post('/users', asyncHandler(async (req: Request, res: Response) => { const input: CreateUserInput = req.body; const user = await createUserWithPassword(input); ... }))` — raw body accepted without any auth check.
findings.recommendation: Add a `requireServiceToken` middleware that validates a shared secret or JWT service token. Pattern: `router.use(requireServiceToken)` at line 31. The auth-service's own jwtService.ts already has `generateServiceToken` — use the complementary `verifyServiceToken` for validation.
findings.impact: Complete takeover of the RBAC system. Attacker can create a user with SUPERADMIN role, then mint JWTs for themselves.

findings.title: payment-service getSellPaymentById and getSellPaymentByOrderId queries lack store_id filter enabling cross-store payment data access
findings.description: Two payment-service query functions fetch sell_payment records WITHOUT store_id filtering: (1) `getSellPaymentById` (line 136-140): `SELECT * FROM payments.sell_payments WHERE id = $1` — any caller with a payment ID can access ANY store's payment data. (2) `getSellPaymentByOrderId` (line 145-149): `SELECT * FROM payments.sell_payments WHERE upi_order_id = $1` — same issue with UPI order IDs. The payment records contain sensitive financial data (amounts, UPI VPAs, transaction references). While payment-service currently only exposes health routes, these query functions are exported and will be called by future route handlers.
findings.evidence: Line 137: `const sql = \`SELECT * FROM payments.sell_payments WHERE id = $1\`;` — no AND store_id = $2 clause. Line 146: `const sql = \`SELECT * FROM payments.sell_payments WHERE upi_order_id = $1\`;` — same pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add store_id as a required parameter to both functions: `getSellPaymentById(paymentId: string, storeId: string)` with `WHERE id = $1 AND store_id = $2`. Apply the same pattern to `completeSellPayment`, `failSellPayment`, and `updateSellPaymentWithOrder`.
findings.impact: Cross-store payment data leakage when payment routes are implemented. Financial data (amounts, VPAs) from any store accessible by knowing a payment ID.

findings.title: supplier-service auth registration has weaker password policy than main auth-service (8 chars only vs 8+letter+number+common-blocklist)
findings.dedupeCheck: Searched 'supplier.*password.*weak', 'supplier.*password.*strength', 'supplier.*password.*8' — no matches. R5.BE.010 covers rate limiting only, not password policy.
findings.description: The supplier-service auth registration (line 142-149) validates password with ONLY `body.password.length < 8`. The main auth-service's userService.ts requires: (1) minimum 8 characters, (2) at least one letter AND one number, (3) NOT in a common password blocklist. This means suppliers can register with passwords like 'aaaaaaaa' (8 a's), '12345678' (numeric only), 'password' (common blocklist), 'qwerty12' (may be in blocklist) — all of which would be rejected by the main auth-service. This creates a security inconsistency where supplier accounts have weaker credentials than retailer accounts.
findings.evidence: Line 143: `if (body.password.length < 8) { throw new ApiError(422, ERROR_CODES.VALIDATION_ERROR, 'Password must be at least 8 characters'); }`
findings.recommendation: Extract the main auth-service's password validation logic into a shared utility in @supermandi/common and use it in both auth flows. At minimum, add: `/^(?=.*[a-zA-Z])(?=.*\d)/.test(body.password)` and a common password blocklist check.
findings.impact: Supplier accounts vulnerable to brute-force and credential stuffing attacks due to weak password requirements.

findings.title: supplier-service auth has no refresh token mechanism — 24-hour access tokens cannot be revoked until expiry
findings.dedupeCheck: Searched 'supplier.*refresh', 'supplier.*token.*rotation', 'supplier.*no.*refresh' — no matches. R5.BE.023 covers actorType casing only.
findings.description: The supplier-service auth issues a single JWT access token with 24-hour expiry (line 104: `expiresIn: '24h'`) but provides NO refresh token mechanism and NO token revocation capability. The main auth-service implements: (1) short-lived access tokens + long-lived refresh tokens, (2) refresh token rotation, (3) idle timeout, (4) session management (list/revoke), (5) Redis blacklist for immediate revocation. Supplier tokens have NONE of these. If a supplier account is compromised, the attacker has 24 hours of irrevocable access. The `generateSupplierToken` function (line 91-107) also doesn't set a `jti` claim, making it impossible to add blacklisting later without code changes.
findings.evidence: Line 103-106: `return jwt.sign(payload, config.jwtSecret, { expiresIn: '24h', issuer: JWT_ISSUER });` — no jti, no refresh token issued alongside. Line 340: `const token = generateSupplierToken(supplier.id, supplier.primary_email);` — only one token returned.
findings.recommendation: Implement refresh token rotation for supplier auth, matching the main auth-service pattern. At minimum: (1) reduce access token expiry to 15-30 minutes, (2) issue a refresh token, (3) add jti claim for blacklisting capability, (4) add a /auth/refresh endpoint.
findings.impact: 24-hour irrevocable access window if a supplier token is leaked or account is compromised.

findings.title: inventory-service getAllStockBalancesForStore returns unbounded result set without pagination or LIMIT clause
findings.dedupeCheck: Searched 'inventory.*no.*pagination', 'inventory.*unbounded', 'getAllStock.*no.*limit' — no matches. Dedupe entry for 'inventory table sorting client-side' (line 2636) is a frontend-only finding.
findings.description: The `getAllStockBalancesForStore` function (lines 174-187) executes `SELECT ... FROM inventory.stock_balances WHERE store_id = $1 ORDER BY product_id` with NO LIMIT clause. This query is called from the route GET /stores/:storeId/inventory (inventory.ts line 62-67) which also applies no pagination. A store with 10,000+ products would return all stock balances in a single response, causing: (1) memory pressure on the Node.js process, (2) large response payload transferred over the network, (3) slow query on large tables. The route also doesn't validate or cap the user-supplied `limit` parameter for `/recent` (line 91: `parseInt(req.query.limit as string, 10) || 100`) — a user could pass `limit=999999`.
findings.evidence: Lines 175-186: `return query<StockBalance>(`SELECT ... FROM inventory.stock_balances WHERE store_id = $1 ORDER BY product_id`, [storeId]);` — no LIMIT. Route line 63-66: `const balances = await listStoreInventory(req.params.storeId); res.json({ data: balances });` — no pagination wrapper.
findings.recommendation: Add pagination parameters (limit/offset) to getAllStockBalancesForStore with a max cap (e.g., 500). Add `Math.min(parseInt(...), 1000)` cap to the /recent endpoint's limit parameter. The route should return pagination metadata (total, limit, offset, hasMore).
findings.impact: OOM risk or slow response for stores with large catalogs. Potential DoS vector if attacker enumerates stores.

findings.title: inventory-service transaction route accepts any transactionType string without enum validation
findings.description: The POST /stores/:storeId/inventory/transactions route (lines 97-128) accepts `body.transactionType` directly from request body and passes it to `createTransaction` without validating it against the allowed enum values ('sale', 'sale_return', 'purchase_received', 'adjustment', 'opening_stock'). The TypeScript type `TransactionType` only provides compile-time checking, not runtime validation. An attacker could send `transactionType: 'foo'` which would either: (1) be inserted into the DB if the column has no CHECK constraint, creating invalid ledger data, or (2) cause a DB error that propagates as a 500 instead of a clean 400 validation error. Similarly, `referenceType` is not validated at the route level.
findings.evidence: Line 100: `const body = req.body as TransactionRequestBody;` — type assertion, not runtime validation. Line 106: `transactionType: body.transactionType` — passed directly to service.
findings.recommendation: Add runtime validation: `const VALID_TYPES: TransactionType[] = ['sale', 'sale_return', 'purchase_received', 'adjustment', 'opening_stock']; if (!VALID_TYPES.includes(body.transactionType)) throw new ApiError(400, 'VALIDATION_ERROR', 'Invalid transactionType');`. Same for referenceType.
findings.impact: Invalid data in inventory_ledger or unclear 500 errors instead of descriptive 400 validation errors.

findings.title: order-service receive.ts GET routes have no authentication middleware — receive history accessible without auth
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.002 covers 'GRN receive routes have NO service-level authentication' (status=done) and R5.BE.020 covers 'getReceiveRecords queries by order_id alone without store_id filter' (status=done). However, those findings were about the POST route and the query-level isolation. The GET routes at lines 127-179 still have NO per-route auth middleware even after R5.BE.002 was resolved — the R5.BE.002 fix may have only addressed the POST route. This is a residual gap.
findings.description: The receive.ts router defines three routes: POST /stores/:storeId/orders/:orderId/receive (lines 42-121) has idempotency middleware, but the GET routes at lines 127-143 (GET /receives) and 149-179 (GET /receives/:receiveId) have NO authentication middleware. The router itself (line 14: `const router: RouterType = Router()`) applies no router-level middleware. While the gateway may protect these routes, defense-in-depth requires service-level auth. Any internal caller or misconfigured gateway route can read GRN receive history.
findings.evidence: Line 127-129: `router.get('/stores/:storeId/orders/:orderId/receives', async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {` — no authenticate/requireStoreAccess middleware. Same pattern at line 149.
findings.recommendation: Add `authenticate` and `requireStoreAccess` from '@supermandi/auth-service/exports' as middleware to both GET routes, matching the pattern used in purchaseOrders.ts and other service routes.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated access to GRN receive records (quantities received, dates, user IDs) from within the service network.

findings.title: GRN receiveGoods inventory HTTP calls occur BEFORE DB transaction creating irreversible partial state on DB failure
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.005 'GRN receiveGoods calls inventory HTTP BEFORE DB commit causing stock updated but order fails inconsistency' (status=done). HOWEVER, code review shows the issue is STILL PRESENT in the source at HEAD 1056e999. The inventory calls happen at lines 225-254 BEFORE `const client = await getClient()` at line 257 and `BEGIN` at line 260. R5.BE.005 was marked 'done' but the code has NOT been fixed.
findings.description: Despite R5.BE.005 being marked 'done', the grnService.ts code at HEAD still calls `callInventoryService()` for each item (lines 225-254) BEFORE beginning the DB transaction (line 260). If the inventory calls succeed but the subsequent DB transaction fails (e.g., constraint violation, deadlock, connection loss), the stock has been increased in inventory-service but no GRN receive record exists in order-service. The idempotency key (line 92: `grn-${referenceSubId}-${productId}`) would prevent a retry from re-adding stock, but the order would show no receive record — creating a permanent inconsistency between inventory and order state.
findings.evidence: Line 225-254: inventory calls in a loop, each calling `callInventoryService()`. Line 257: `const client = await getClient();` — DB client acquired AFTER inventory calls. Line 260: `await client.query('BEGIN');` — transaction starts after stock already changed.
findings.recommendation: Restructure to: (1) BEGIN transaction first, (2) create receive record and update order items, (3) call inventory-service, (4) if inventory fails ROLLBACK the DB transaction, (5) COMMIT only if both succeed. Alternatively, use a saga pattern with compensating transactions.
findings.impact: Permanent stock/order inconsistency if DB transaction fails after inventory was updated. Cannot be fixed by retry due to idempotency keys.

findings.title: reorder-service policy CRUD by ID routes still lack store isolation despite R5.BE.006 marked done
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.006 'Policy CRUD by ID has no store ownership verification' (status=done). HOWEVER, code review at HEAD 1056e999 shows the GET /policies/:policyId (line 136-160), PUT /policies/:policyId (line 233-255), and DELETE /policies/:policyId (line 261-277) routes STILL have no requireStoreAccess middleware and no store isolation check. R5.BE.006 was marked 'done' but the code has NOT been fixed.
findings.description: Three routes in the reorder-service policies.ts access policies by policyId without any store isolation: (1) GET /policies/:policyId (line 136-160): Retrieves any policy by ID regardless of store ownership. (2) PUT /policies/:policyId (line 233-255): Updates any policy by ID — an authenticated user from store A can modify store B's reorder policies. (3) DELETE /policies/:policyId (line 261-277): Deletes any policy by ID. The router-level `authenticate` middleware (line 21) ensures the user is logged in, but these three routes don't use `requireStoreAccess` and don't check that the policy's storeId matches the authenticated user's store. Compare to the store-scoped routes (lines 37-67, 69-99, 105-130, 173-221, 290-336) which correctly use `requireStoreAccess`.
findings.evidence: Line 233-235: `router.put('/policies/:policyId', async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {` — no requireStoreAccess. Line 240: `const policy = await updatePolicyService(policyId, {...})` — updates without store check.
findings.recommendation: Either: (1) Add requireStoreAccess and validate policy.storeId matches request storeId, or (2) Replace these non-store-scoped routes with store-scoped equivalents like PUT /stores/:storeId/policies/:policyId with requireStoreAccess. The PATCH route at line 290-336 already demonstrates the correct pattern with store ownership verification.
findings.impact: Cross-store policy manipulation. Authenticated user from any store can read/modify/delete reorder policies of any other store.

findings.title: payment-service has no API routes exposing payment operations — db queries exist but no route handlers create/read/update payments
findings.description: The payment-service entry point (index.ts line 25) only mounts health routes: `app.use('/', healthRoutes)`. The service has complete db query functions for sell_payments (create, update, complete, fail, get by ID, get by order ID), buy_payments (create, update, complete), and BNPL drawdowns (create, list) — but NONE of these are exposed via HTTP routes. The Razorpay client has order creation, payment fetching, signature verification, payout creation, fund account and contact management — all unreachable. This means the entire payment system is a dead-code scaffold that cannot be called by any other service or client.
findings.evidence: index.ts line 25: `app.use('/', healthRoutes);` — only route mount. db/queries.ts has 7 export functions (createSellPayment, updateSellPaymentWithOrder, completeSellPayment, failSellPayment, getSellPaymentById, getSellPaymentByOrderId, createBuyPayment, etc.) — none wired to routes.
findings.recommendation: Implement route handlers for payment operations. At minimum: POST /payments/sell (create), POST /payments/sell/:id/complete, GET /payments/sell/:id, POST /payments/buy (create). All routes need auth middleware and store_id scoping on every query.
findings.impact: No payment functionality available despite code existing. UPI collection/payout, BNPL features are dead code.

findings.title: voice-service /status/:requestId endpoint has no auth middleware and leaks transcript data to any caller
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.007 'No auth middleware: /status/:requestId leaks voice transcripts' (status=done). HOWEVER, code review at HEAD shows the GET /status/:requestId route (lines 295-320) STILL has no authentication check and no store isolation. R5.BE.007 was marked 'done' but the code has NOT been fixed.
findings.description: The GET /status/:requestId route (lines 295-320) returns voice request data including transcript text, parsed intent, and execution status without any authentication. The /interpret and /execute endpoints correctly check `req.headers['x-actor-id']` for store context, but /status does not. Anyone who guesses or intercepts a requestId (UUID) can read the voice transcript. The /execute endpoint (line 217) validates store ownership (`voiceRequest.storeId !== storeId`), but /status skips this check entirely.
findings.evidence: Line 295-297: `router.get('/status/:requestId', async (req: Request, res: Response): Promise<void> => {` — no auth check. Line 310-316: returns `transcript`, `intent`, `executed`, `createdAt` — sensitive data.
findings.recommendation: Add store context validation: extract `x-actor-id` from headers, verify it matches `voiceRequest.storeId` before returning data. If the header is missing, return 401.
findings.impact: Voice transcripts (potentially containing product names, quantities, business data) leaked to unauthenticated callers.

findings.title: inventory-service recent activity endpoint accepts unbounded limit parameter — no max cap
findings.description: The GET /stores/:storeId/inventory/recent route (lines 88-95) parses a user-supplied `limit` query parameter with `parseInt(req.query.limit as string, 10) || 100` but applies NO upper bound. A client can request `limit=1000000` and the query will attempt to return 1 million ledger entries from the inventory_ledger table. The same pattern exists in GET /stores/:storeId/inventory/low-stock (threshold at line 77 has no upper limit but is less dangerous) and GET /stores/:storeId/inventory/:productId/history (line 117 with default 50, also uncapped).
findings.evidence: Line 91: `const limit = parseInt(req.query.limit as string, 10) || 100;` — no `Math.min(...)` cap. Line 92: `const entries = await getStoreRecentActivity(req.params.storeId, limit);` — passed directly to DB query.
findings.recommendation: Add `Math.min(limit, 1000)` or similar cap. Pattern: `const limit = Math.min(parseInt(req.query.limit as string, 10) || 100, 1000);`. Apply to all three routes that accept a limit parameter.
findings.impact: Memory exhaustion on large stores. DoS vector for authenticated users.

findings.title: platform-service stores routes have no defense-in-depth authentication despite handling CRUD on all stores
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.003 'Platform stores CRUD has NO service-level authentication' (status=done). HOWEVER, code review at HEAD shows stores.ts STILL has no authentication middleware at lines 16-122. The comment at line 88 says 'requires SUPERADMIN - enforced by gateway' but there is no service-level check. R5.BE.003 was marked 'done' but the code has NOT been fixed.
findings.description: All platform-service store routes (GET /, GET /:storeId, POST /, PUT /:storeId, DELETE /:storeId) have no authentication middleware. The router at line 16 is a bare `Router()` with no `.use()` calls for auth. POST creates stores, PUT updates any store, DELETE removes stores — all relying solely on the API gateway for access control. If the gateway misconfigures a route or if the service is accessed directly (e.g., within the VPC), anyone can create/modify/delete stores.
findings.evidence: Line 16: `const router: Router = Router();` — no auth middleware. Line 88-97: `router.post('/', asyncHandler(async (req: Request, res: Response) => { const input = req.body as CreateStoreInput; const store = await createNewStore(input); ... }))` — comment says 'requires SUPERADMIN - enforced by gateway' but no code check.
findings.recommendation: Add `authenticate` and role-checking middleware. For GET routes, at minimum verify the caller is authenticated. For POST/PUT/DELETE, verify SUPERADMIN role at the service level.
findings.impact: Unauthorized store creation/modification/deletion if gateway is bypassed or misconfigured.

findings.title: order-service getReceiveRecords and getReceiveRecordItems queries use orderId without store_id filter
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.020 'getReceiveRecords queries by order_id alone without store_id filter' (status=done). However, code review at HEAD shows the GET routes still pass only orderId to getReceiveRecords (line 133) and getReceiveRecordItems (line 166) without storeId. The storeId URL parameter is captured but NOT passed to the query functions.
findings.description: The GET /stores/:storeId/orders/:orderId/receives route (line 127-143) captures `storeId` from URL params but only passes `orderId` to `getReceiveRecords(orderId)` at line 133. The storeId is completely ignored in the query, meaning a user from store A could access store B's receive records by guessing an orderId. The same applies to GET /receives/:receiveId at line 155 where `getReceiveRecords(orderId)` is called without storeId.
findings.evidence: Line 131: `const { orderId } = req.params;` — storeId destructured but not used. Line 133: `const records = await getReceiveRecords(orderId);` — storeId not passed.
findings.recommendation: Pass storeId to getReceiveRecords and add WHERE store_id = $2 to the underlying query. Same for getReceiveRecordItems.
findings.impact: Cross-store GRN receive record access. An authenticated user can read any store's receive history by knowing an orderId.

findings.title: supplier-service CSV product upload silently skips conflicts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — no error count returned to caller
findings.description: The CSV bulk upload endpoint for supplier products uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (approximately line 731) when inserting products in batches of 100. When a conflict occurs (e.g., duplicate barcode or SKU), the row is silently skipped. The API response does not differentiate between successfully inserted rows and skipped conflicts. A supplier uploading 500 products where 200 have duplicate barcodes would see '500 processed' without knowing 200 were skipped. This can lead to confusion about which products were actually added and which need manual correction.
findings.evidence: INSERT statement uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — conflicting rows are silently dropped without counting or reporting.
findings.recommendation: Change to `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id` and count the actual inserted rows. Return both `totalProcessed` and `totalInserted` in the response. Optionally collect skipped barcodes/SKUs for the conflict report.
findings.impact: Silent data loss during bulk uploads. Suppliers believe products were added when they were actually skipped due to conflicts.

findings.title: retailerPortal daily-summary endpoint trusts client-supplied date parameter without validation allowing arbitrary date range queries
findings.description: The GET /retailer-admin/daily-summary endpoint (lines 237-334) accepts an optional `date` query parameter that is passed directly to `new Date(date as string)` at line 245 without format validation. While the store_id is correctly derived from JWT via getRetailerContext(), the date parameter could be: (1) Invalid strings like 'foo' → `new Date('foo')` produces 'Invalid Date' which `.toISOString()` throws on, causing an unhandled 500 error. (2) Very old dates like '1900-01-01' or future dates like '2099-01-01' — while harmless for data, they waste DB resources on pointless queries. The IST timezone conversion at line 247 also has a subtle issue: `new Date(new Date().toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }))` creates a date that's offset by the server's timezone, which may be incorrect in Cloud Run (UTC).
findings.evidence: Line 245: `const targetDate = date ? new Date(date as string) : new Date(new Date().toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }));` — no format validation on date input.
findings.recommendation: Validate date format: `if (date && !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(date as string)) throw ApiError.badRequest('Invalid date format, use YYYY-MM-DD');`. For IST handling, use a proper timezone library or `Intl.DateTimeFormat`.
findings.impact: 500 errors on malformed dates. Minor risk of incorrect daily summaries if timezone handling differs between dev and production.

findings.title: voice-service in-memory request store has no size limit — can grow unbounded under sustained load
findings.dedupeCheck: R5.BE.016 covers 'In-memory Map for voice request state incompatible with Cloud Run multi-instance' (status=done). This finding adds a NEW dimension: the Map has no size limit. While R5.BE.016 addresses the multi-instance issue, the unbounded growth issue is separate.
findings.description: The voice-service requestStore (line 57: `const requestStore = new Map<string, VoiceRequest>()`) has a cleanup interval of 5 minutes (lines 60-67) that removes entries older than 5 minutes. However, there is no maximum size limit on the Map. During peak load, if many voice requests arrive within a 5-minute window, the Map grows without bound. Each VoiceRequest stores the full transcript text and parsed intent. A burst of 100,000 requests in 5 minutes (e.g., DDoS or misbehaving client) would consume significant memory. The cleanup only runs at 5-minute intervals, not on insertion, so the Map can grow to any size between cleanups.
findings.evidence: Line 57: `const requestStore = new Map<string, VoiceRequest>();` — no size limit. Lines 60-67: cleanup runs on setInterval, not on insertion.
findings.recommendation: Add a size check before insertion: `if (requestStore.size >= 10000) { /* reject or evict oldest */ }`. Consider using an LRU cache library like `lru-cache` with maxSize.
findings.impact: Memory exhaustion under sustained load. Node.js process OOM kill on Cloud Run.

findings.title: api-gateway Redis token blacklist fail-open behavior allows revoked tokens through when Redis is down
findings.dedupeCheck: Searched 'redis.*fail.*open', 'blacklist.*fail', 'token.*revoc.*redis.*down' — no matches. The existing T-184 ticket in dedupe_index covers implementing the blacklist, not the fail-open behavior.
findings.description: The jwtAuth middleware's Redis blacklist check (lines 220-237) catches errors and fails open: `catch (blacklistError) { console.warn('[T-184] Redis blacklist check failed (failing open):', blacklistError); }`. The comment at line 234-235 says 'downstream services still check DB-based revocation as a fallback'. However, this DB-based fallback is NOT implemented in any downstream service routes — the auth-service's refresh token revocation only blocks new access token generation, it doesn't validate existing access tokens on every request. This means if Redis goes down, ALL previously revoked tokens become valid again for the remainder of their expiry window (up to 24 hours for supplier tokens).
findings.evidence: Lines 233-237: `} catch (blacklistError) { console.warn('[T-184] Redis blacklist check failed (failing open):', blacklistError); }` — silently allows revoked tokens through. No downstream DB fallback exists.
findings.recommendation: Document the fail-open trade-off explicitly. Consider fail-closed for high-security paths (e.g., /platform, /retailer-admin/stores). Implement the referenced 'DB-based revocation fallback' in downstream services, or at minimum add a DB check in the gateway when Redis is unavailable.
findings.impact: Revoked tokens remain valid during Redis outage. Logged-out users retain access. Compromised tokens cannot be invalidated.
